Bob Fosse was an American choreographer, dancer, and director who created a distinctive theatrical style blending jazz, vaudeville, and contemporary movement. Born in Chicago in nineteen twenty-seven, he trained in vaudeville and burlesque before breaking into Broadway in the nineteen fifties. He developed the Fosse technique, marked by flexed wrists, hunched shoulders, splayed hands, and intricate footwork performed with seeming casualness and dark humor—a style characterized by turned-in knees, angular arm positions, and sharp isolations that transformed both Broadway musicals and film. He choreographed and directed Chicago in nineteen seventy-five, which revived the musical theater and won the Tony Award for Best Musical, his staging becoming a benchmark for theatrical innovation. In nineteen seventy-three alone, he won an unprecedented three Tony Awards for choreography and direction of Pippin and A Little Night Music, establishing him as Broadway's pre-eminent figure. He directed the film Cabaret in nineteen seventy-two, whose choreography revolutionized how dance was integrated into cinema—the film itself won eight Academy Awards. He later created All That Jazz in nineteen seventy-nine, a semi-autobiographical film that blended his dance vocabulary with existential filmmaking to become a cult classic. Throughout his work, he was known for incorporating sexuality, irony, and darkness into musical theater, breaking the bright, optimistic conventions of mid-century Broadway.
